title: The ambrosial hour
hook: Sikhs rise before dawn for prayer and meditation

segments.voice: Yesterday, the guru: a teacher whose words carry weight, and the two tests, do they know it, do they live it. Your line was choose with care. Whose advice did you weigh before taking it? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-nine.

An alarm goes off with nothing scheduled after it. No meeting, no shift, no school bell. Someone gets up anyway, washes, wraps a turban or covers their hair, and sits down on the floor with a small book, or walks to the gurdwara, where the doors are already open. Outside, the birds haven't started. The day hasn't asked for anything yet. That's the point. Today's path turns from Hindu ways to Sikh ways, and it starts before the sun. Today's word is the name for that hour: amrit vela.
screen: `AN ALARM, NOTHING SCHEDULED.` → `THE DOORS ARE ALREADY OPEN.` → `THE DAY HASN'T ASKED YET.`

segments.voice: Amrit vela: the ambrosial hour, the early hours before dawn. Amrit is nectar, the drink of immortality, and it's also the word Sikhs use for the sweetened water of initiation. Vela is the time, the hour. Put together: the nectar time. Where does it come from? Right at the start of the Guru Granth Sahib, in Guru Nanak's Japji, the fourth stanza names it. In the ambrosial hours, it says, in paraphrase, meditate on the true Name, and reflect on God's greatness. Two jobs for the early hour: remember the Name, and consider how great is the one it names. A later Guru, Guru Ram Das, is even more practical. In a passage of the Guru Granth Sahib he describes someone who calls themselves a Sikh of the true Guru. That person, he says, rises early and meditates on the Name. Makes the effort in the early morning, and bathes in the pool of nectar. And then goes on through the day singing the Guru's word. Notice the order. In the passage, the early hour isn't an escape from the day. It's the start of it. The ambrosial hour comes first, and the day is meant to carry what was found there. And why so early? The texts don't give a lecture on it. But the hour has its own texture. The phone hasn't buzzed. Nobody needs you. The mind hasn't filled up yet. Whatever you put in first, it seems, has room.
screen: `AMRIT VELA: THE NECTAR TIME.` · `JAPJI: THE NAME, AND GOD'S GREATNESS.` · `RISE EARLY, BATHE, REMEMBER.` · `THE START OF THE DAY, NOT AN ESCAPE.` · then, large: `WHAT GOES IN FIRST HAS ROOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, in two halves. Now, sit as if it were that hour. Dim a light if you can, settle, and let the breath slow. Notice what the room sounds like when it isn't asking for anything. If you pray, you can remember a name of God you hold dear. If you don't, just sit in the quiet. Then, before the bell, decide one thing: tomorrow, or one day this week, you'll wake early once, even fifteen minutes, and give those first minutes to stillness before the phone. The bell holds the time.
Amrit vela. The ambrosial hour before dawn, when Sikhs who keep it rise to remember the Name before the day begins asking. Today's word.
Your line: the early hour. Set the alarm tonight a little earlier, and tomorrow give the first quiet minutes to stillness before anything else gets in. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the amrit vela rise in the hours before dawn, bathe, and give the time to meditation on the Name and the morning prayers, at home or in the gurdwara, before the work of the day.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: the ambrosial hour before dawn, from Japji.

trapdoor: what you thought: amrit vela is getting up early to be productive.
what it means: the ambrosial hour before dawn, kept for remembering the Name before the day begins.
what a scholar hears: Japji stanza four sets the amrit vela for the true Name and God's greatness; Guru Ram Das (Guru Granth Sahib 305) describes the Sikh who rises early to meditate on the Name.

sources.ref: Gauri ki Var, Guru Ram Das (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 305–306)

notes: Japji pauri 4 ('amrit vela sach nao vadiai vichar') paraphrased; Macauliffe 1909 wording not checked.

Guru Ram Das, Ang 305–306 ('gur satgur ka jo sikh akhae...') paraphrased: rising early, effort, bathing in the pool of nectar, meditating on the Name, then singing the Guru's word through the day. Confirm.
'Amrit: nectar, the drink of immortality; also the initiation water' and 'vela: time' are given as meanings; confirm under the etymology rule.
'Sikh teaching doesn't ask anyone to leave home for a cave; Sikhs work, raise families and run shops' summarizes the householder ideal; confirm phrasing.
Practice suggests 'even fifteen minutes' earlier as an everyday suggestion, not a tradition claim.
Day marks the block's turn from Hindu ways to Sikh ways.
